doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: Rejecting Thelonious Monk and playing opposite him at the Five Spot
summary: Israels asks a host to turn off a Monk record, admits he dismissed Monk's music, and recalls weeks with Timmons' trio opposite Monk at the Five Spot.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: Yeah. I also have had the experience of being at a party where I was specifically invited, graciously, as a new faculty member by another faculty member wanting to introduce me to his friends and make me feel welcome. And I’m at this party at this nice guy’s house and he’s playing a Monk record. And we’re standing around having a conversation and I go up to Milt and say, “ Gee Milt, please turn that off. I can’t talk to people, I have to listen to that. It’s not background to me.”
Interesting. And there was a time when you didn’t like Thelonious Monk, isn’t that true?

That’s right. That’s right. Absolutely. I was terribly — I rejected that music out of hand and incorrectly and stupidly or ignorantly and that is — I lost a lot of time appreciating that and being around him when I could have been paying attention and taking a lot more in and getting a lot more value out of being in the band playing opposite his band. I played with Bobby Timmon’s trio opposite Monk’s quartet at the Five Spot in New York for weeks and weeks.
Did you listen to his music in that particular situation with the idea that what would I do if I was his bass player?

No. I didn’t get that far. I was — some people have, when I’ve talked to them about this have excused me, probably realistically, by saying, “Of course you were focused on a particular thing. You were trying to understand and become conversant in the language of Bill Evans, Tommy Flanagan, Hank Jones, Sonny Clark were the piano players for example. And the piano playing language of Monk was so — at least superficially — diametrically opposed to that, that you couldn’t take it in. You couldn’t see — that was banging. You didn’t want banging, you wanted — well okay, it is banging — he does bang the piano. The fact is he banged the piano in the most incredibly artistic and effective and creative and personal way that I now appreciate with almost worshipful understanding. I didn’t at the time, but okay. Fortunately it happened before I died.
